**The "I" is not a construction** We have established knowledge and memory. Now Abhinavagupta takes up the third power — the apohana, the removal — that serves both. And at its heart lies a question that threatens the whole doctrine. The reflexive-awareness, we have said, is the manifestation's own nature. But the reflexive-awareness is word-joined; and the word-joined, it might seem, is a construction (vikalpa). If so, then the Lord's own self-awareness would be a construction — which cannot be. The construction is of the māyā-form, the saṃsāric; how could it be in the Lord? Kārikā 1 answers this, and its answer is precise. The "I"-recollection (ahaṃ-pratyavamarśa) — even though it has the word as its body — is *not* a construction. It is the fit, the two-throwing, the determination. Consider what the pure "I"-recollection is. It is the self-grasp of the manifestation free of the contraction by the body and the rest — the grasp of the self-nature, resting in the freedom, supreme, foundational: the "I." This, Abhinavagupta insists, is not a construction. And to see why, we must ask what a construction actually is. The construction (vikalpa, the vivida-kalpanā) is of three kinds: it joins what is distinct (as one joins molasses, curd, and pepper into a compound); it constructs the one in many ways; or it splits off a doubted, other form. All three are operations of division and joining, of this-and-that. But the "I"-recollection is none of these. It does not join a distinct "this" to a distinct "I"; it is the single self-grasp, resting in itself. It does not construct the one into many; it is the one. It does not split off a doubted other; it is the un-doubted foundation. The "I" is not built up out of parts, nor split out of a doubt — it is the pure self-awareness that underlies every construction, the very thing that makes construction possible, without itself being one. This is the apohanaśakti at its root. The removal — the power by which the self excludes what is not itself — is not a construction that the self performs upon itself; it is the self's own grasp, the pure "I" that, in knowing itself, is the foundation of all the word-joined, constructed dealings of the world. And this pure "I"-recollection, resting in the freedom, is the Lord's self-awareness — not a māyā-form construction, but the very nature of the manifestation, the self-grasp that is the Lord. The apohana, the removal, is not a cutting off; it is the self's own luminous grasp, the "I" that is one, un-divided, and free. ---

> The claim is that the essence of light is the reflexive awareness, not the bare showing of objects. > The crystal supplies the contrast: a light that merely showed the world without knowing that it showed > it would be no different from crystal — it would reflect, but be inert. What makes the light conscious > is the self-awareness in the very act of manifesting. The passage then identifies this self-knowing > with the supreme speech (parā-vāk) and with the Lord's freedom and lordship. > > The identification with the Word is the extension: the reflexivity is not a bare self-presence but > the supreme speech from which the lower levels of language descend. This is why the word-joined "I" > need not be a construction — language is the form the self-grasp takes, not something that produces > it. The passage establishes the reflexivity claim; the full account of the powers and the Lordship is > developed in the following vimarśas. parā-vāk (supreme speech) · svātantrya/aiśvarya (freedom/lordship).
